messages.content: I don't want the nurse to check on me tonight. I just want to sleep.

I get it — you really want a good sleep, and being woken up isn't fun. The nurses do come by at night to make sure you're safe and comfy, but they try to be really quiet and quick so you can go back to sleep fast. You could ask your nurse if you can have a small nightlight or your favourite blanket to help you feel cozy when they come in. You're doing a great job resting here.
My mom had to leave and I'm scared to be here alone.

It's really okay to feel scared when your mom isn't here. She let the nurses know she had to step out, and they're keeping a close eye on you while she's away. You can press the call button any time you need something or just want to talk to someone. Your mom will be back, and the people here are looking out for you the whole time.
Why does my room smell weird? I don't like it here.

Hospital rooms can smell different from home, and it's totally fine that you don't love it. The smell comes from the cleaning stuff they use to keep everything really clean and safe for you. If you brought anything from home like a favourite stuffed animal or blanket, keeping it close can help your room feel more like yours. You could also ask your parent to bring something small that smells nice and familiar — just nothing with perfume since the hospital is fragrance-free.
I heard a loud beeping sound and it scared me.

That beeping can definitely be surprising! Machines in the hospital make sounds to let the nurses know things like when a bag of fluid is finished or when something needs a quick check. It doesn't mean something bad is happening — it's kind of like a little alarm clock reminding the nurse to come over. If you hear it again and feel worried, you can tell your nurse and they'll explain what that specific beep means.
I miss my dog so much. Can he come visit me?

Aww, missing your dog makes total sense — pets are such good friends. Regular pet visits aren't usually allowed at the hospital because they want to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But there is good news: the hospital has therapy dogs from St. John Ambulance that visit sometimes! You could ask your Child Life Specialist if there's a therapy dog visit coming up. You could also ask your family to send you a photo or video of your dog to watch when you miss them.
I don't want them to look at my armband again. They keep checking it.

I know it probably feels like a lot when people keep looking at your armband. They do it because it has your name and other important stuff on it, and checking it is how they make sure you always get exactly the right care. It's actually a really good thing — it means everyone is being extra careful with you. You're being so patient about it, and that's awesome.
I can't play with the other kids because I have to stay in my room. It's not fair.

You're right, that doesn't feel fair, and it's okay to be upset about it. Sometimes the doctors need you to stay in your room for a little while to keep you and the other kids safe. But there are still fun things you can do! You could ask about the art therapy program or see if a Child Life Specialist can bring you some activities. There's also a music therapist who can come to your room. You won't be stuck in your room with nothing to do — there are people here whose whole job is helping kids have a better time.
What if the doctors can't fix me?

That's a really big worry, and I'm glad you told me about it. It's normal to think about things like that when you're in the hospital. There's a whole team of people here — doctors, nurses, and lots of other helpers — all working together to take the best care of you. If you're feeling scared, talking to your parent or your nurse about how you feel can help a lot. You could also talk to a Child Life Specialist — they're really good at helping kids with big worries like this.
I'm going to miss my best friend's birthday party because I'm stuck here.

Oh no, that's really disappointing. Missing something special like a birthday party is hard, and it's okay to feel sad about it. Maybe you and your family could think of a way to still be part of it — like a video call during the party or making a card in the activity room on the sixth floor to give your friend later. Your friend will understand, and you two can have your own celebration when you're feeling better.
The hospital food doesn't taste like my mom's cooking. I want to go home.

I bet your mom's cooking is way better — home food is always special. Wanting to go home is one of the most normal feelings ever when you're in the hospital. The good news is your family can bring you some of your favourite foods and keep them in the family fridge on your floor, as long as your care team says it's okay for you to eat them. And every single day you're here, you're getting closer to going home to all your favourite meals.
Why do I have to wear this bracelet on my arm?

That bracelet is really important! It has your name and birthday on it, plus a special barcode. Before anyone gives you medicine or does a test, they check your bracelet to make absolutely sure they have the right person. Think of it like a VIP pass that tells everyone exactly who you are so they can take the best care of you.
What is the SMILE Room?

The SMILE Room is a super cool room on the sixth floor that's full of things to help you relax or have fun! It has bubble columns with colours moving inside them, fibre optic lights you can touch, mirrors, and music. It's a special place where you can go to feel calm or just enjoy some really neat sensory stuff. You can ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you'd like to visit!
Is there a playground here?

There isn't an outdoor playground, but there are some awesome rooms to play in! There's Ashley's Backyard on the sixth floor, which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids, and there's also a School-Age Activity Room where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and work on puzzles. A grown-up just needs to come with you. Ask your nurse which one you can visit!
Can my dog come visit me?

Regular pet visits aren't allowed at the hospital because they want to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But guess what — sometimes therapy dogs from St. John Ambulance come to visit patients! Those are specially trained dogs that are really gentle. You can ask your care team if a therapy dog visit is coming up soon. That would be pretty exciting, right?
What are Bravery Beads?

Bravery Beads are so cool! Every time something happens during your care — like a test, a treatment, or a procedure — you get a special bead to put on a string. Each kind of bead means something different. Over time, you build this amazing collection that tells the story of how brave you've been. It's like a necklace or keychain that shows everything you've been through. Ask your care team if you'd like to start collecting them!
Who is Ollie?

Ollie is the hospital's very own therapeutic clown! Ollie's whole job is to help kids laugh, play, and have fun while they're in the hospital. Ollie is specially trained to make your day a little brighter and help things feel more normal. If you see Ollie around, you're in for a treat!
Why does everyone keep washing their hands so much?

Great question! Germs are tiny things that are way too small to see, and they can make people sick. In the hospital, washing hands is the number one way to stop germs from spreading from one person to another. That's why your nurses, doctors, and even your visitors clean their hands every time they come into your room and every time they leave. You can help too by washing your hands — especially before you eat!
Can I watch TV?

Yes! The hospital has a special entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. And if your family has a streaming service like Netflix or Disney+, you can log in with your own account and watch that too. Ask your nurse to help you get it set up if you're not sure how!
What does the person in the white coat do?

People in white coats are usually doctors, but sometimes they might be medical students who are still learning to become doctors! They work as a team. The main doctor is called the attending physician, and they're in charge of your care. If a younger person in a white coat comes to check on you, they might be a student or a resident — that's someone who finished medical school and is getting extra training. They all work together to help you feel better.
Where does my food come from in the hospital?

The hospital has its own kitchen called Patient Food Services! They make breakfast, lunch, and dinner for all the patients. Your doctor picks a menu that's right for you, and then you get a form on your breakfast tray where you can choose what you'd like to eat the next day. Breakfast comes in the morning, lunch around noon, and dinner in the late afternoon. If your family wants a snack, there's a Tim Hortons on the second floor too!
Why do I have to wear this bracelet on my arm?

That bracelet is really important! It has your name and birthday on it, and a special barcode. Before the doctors or nurses give you any medicine or do a test, they check your bracelet to make sure everything is exactly right for you. Think of it like a super-special name tag that helps keep you safe the whole time you're here.
Can my mom bring my dog to visit me?

I know you must really miss your dog! Pets from home aren't usually allowed to visit because we need to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But guess what — sometimes specially trained therapy dogs come to visit kids in the hospital! You could ask your nurse if there's a therapy dog visit coming up on your unit. That might be a fun surprise!
I'm hungry. When is dinner?

Dinner trays usually come between 4:45 and 5:45 in the evening. Before you eat anything, though, your nurse needs to say it's okay — sometimes there are special reasons a kid might need to wait. If your tummy is really rumbling and it's not dinnertime yet, ask your parent or guardian to check with your nurse about getting a snack from the pantry.
Why does everyone keep squirting that stuff on their hands?

Great question! That's hand sanitizer, and it kills tiny germs you can't even see. Everybody — nurses, doctors, your family, and visitors — cleans their hands when they come into your room and when they leave. It's one of the best ways to stop germs from spreading so kids like you can get better faster. You can use it too!
Can I go play in the hallway?

The hallways are really busy with carts and people moving around, so it's safest to stay in your room or go to one of the special play spaces. There's a cool activity room on the sixth floor called the School-Age Activity Room where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and lots more. Ask your nurse or your parent if you can go check it out!
Why can't I sleep in the same bed as my mommy?

I know it would feel really cozy to snuggle up together, but the nurses need to be able to reach you quickly whenever they come to check on you, even in the middle of the night. Your mom can sleep right beside you, though — there's a special sleep space for a parent right next to your bed. So she'll be super close all night long.
Can I bring all my stuffed animals?

You can definitely bring a few favourite stuffed animals to help your room feel more like home! The hospital does ask that you don't bring too many, though, because the nurses need space around your bed to take care of you and keep things clean. Pick your top favourites — ones that can be wiped down or washed are the best choice. And remember, your stuffies should stay with you and not be shared with other kids, just to keep everyone healthy.
There's a scary machine that beeps when I walk through the door downstairs. What is it?

That machine is there to help keep everyone in the hospital safe. It checks to make sure nobody is bringing anything inside that could be dangerous. You just walk right through it — you don't have to stop or take anything off. If it makes a little sound, a friendly security guard might take a quick look, but it's nothing to worry about at all. It's kind of like the ones at the airport!
Why do the nurses keep waking me up at night?

I know it can be annoying to get woken up when you're cozy and sleepy! The nurses check on you during the night to make sure you're doing okay — things like making sure you're comfortable and safe. It's actually a really caring thing they do for every kid here. Try to close your eyes again right after and you'll drift back to sleep. You're doing great!
My friend wants to come visit. Can she come whenever she wants?

It's awesome that your friend wants to visit! Visiting times can be a little different depending on which part of the hospital you're in, so the best thing to do is have your parent ask your nurse about the best times for visitors. Also, it's really important that your friend only comes if she's feeling totally healthy — no coughs, sniffles, or tummy bugs. That way everyone stays safe!
Why does someone keep coming to check on me when I'm sleeping?

That's your nurse! Nurses come to check on you during the night to make sure you're comfortable and safe. They might look at a machine near your bed, feel your forehead, or just peek in quietly. They try really hard not to wake you up. It's kind of like how your mom or dad might check on you at home before they go to bed — except nurses do it a few times during the night because that's their special job. If the light or sounds bother you, you can tell your nurse and they'll try to be extra quiet.
What's the bracelet they put on my arm?

That's your hospital armband! It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Every time a nurse or doctor needs to give you medicine or do a test, they'll look at your bracelet to make absolutely sure they have the right kid. You might notice they ask your name and birthday a lot too — that's not because they forgot, it's another way they double-check so you stay safe. You need to keep it on the whole time you're here, but if it feels itchy or too tight, tell your nurse and they can fix it for you.
I'm hungry. When do I get food?

Meals come at set times here at the hospital. Breakfast arrives in the morning, lunch comes around noon, and dinner shows up in the late afternoon. Before your meal, you'll get a little form on your breakfast tray where you can pick what you'd like to eat the next day — kind of like ordering from a menu! But here's one important thing: before you eat or drink anything, your nurse needs to say it's okay. Sometimes doctors need your tummy to be empty for a test or procedure. If you're feeling really hungry between meals, ask your parent to check with your nurse about a snack.
Can my dog come visit me?

I know you must miss your dog a lot! Unfortunately, family pets usually aren't allowed to visit because the hospital needs to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But there is some good news — the hospital has special therapy dogs that sometimes visit kids on certain units. These are friendly, trained dogs from St. John Ambulance who come just to cheer you up! Ask your parent to check with your care team about when the next therapy dog visit might happen. In the meantime, you could bring a photo of your dog or even a stuffed animal that reminds you of them.
There's a sign on my door and people keep putting on gowns. Am I in trouble?

You are definitely not in trouble! That sign means the doctors and nurses are being extra careful to stop germs from spreading. Sometimes when a kid is sick with something that could be passed on, the hospital puts up a sign so everyone remembers to put on special gloves, a gown, or a mask before they come in. It's kind of like putting on a raincoat to keep the rain off — the gown keeps germs from going in or out of the room. Your visitors will need to follow those rules too, but your nurse can show them exactly what to do. It's all about keeping everyone safe.
My room number is B2-503. What does that mean?

Your room number is like a little code that helps everyone find you! Let me break it down: the 'B' means you're in Zone B of the hospital — that's where Children's Hospital is. The '2' means you're on the second floor. And '503' is your actual room number on that floor. So if someone says 'B2-503,' they know exactly which building, which floor, and which room to go to. Pretty cool, right? It's kind of like how your home address has a street name and a house number so people can find where you live.
Why are they putting cream on my arm before the needle?

That cream is something really helpful — it's called a numbing cream! The nurses put it on your skin before a needle so that the spot gets kind of sleepy. When the cream does its job, you feel way less of the poke. This is part of something the hospital calls the Comfort Promise, which means they try really hard to make needles hurt as little as possible for every kid. They might also help you sit in a comfy position or let you watch a video or play with something while it happens. If you're feeling scared, it's totally okay to tell your nurse and they'll help you feel better.
Can I watch TV or play games here?

Yes! The hospital has a special entertainment website where you can watch live TV for free. If your family has a streaming account — like for movies or shows — you can log in and watch your favourite stuff too. There are also some really fun rooms to visit. The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor has crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. It's open during the day and sometimes the Child Life team runs special activities there. There's also a cool room called the SMILE Room that has bubble lights, music, and fibre optics — it's a really neat place to relax.
Why can't I bring my balloon into the hospital?

I know balloons are fun, but the hospital doesn't allow the regular rubbery kind — those are called latex balloons. Some people are really allergic to latex, and it can make them very sick, even if they just breathe near it. So to keep all the kids safe, those balloons have to stay outside. The good news is that foil balloons — the shiny, crinkly kind — are totally fine! So if someone wants to bring you a balloon to make your room cheerful, just let them know to get a foil one instead.
What happens when I get to go home? Do I just leave?

Not quite — but it's exciting news when the doctor says you're ready! Before you leave, your care team will sit down with your parent or guardian and go over everything: what medicines you'll need to take at home, when to come back for a check-up, and what to watch for. Your nurse will make sure your parent has written instructions so nobody has to remember it all in their head. You'll also need your car seat for the ride home — that's the law to keep you safe. Make sure you and your family pack up all your toys and belongings so nothing gets left behind!
Who is the person who keeps coming to check my arm where the tube is?

That's your nurse! You have a nurse who is specially assigned to take care of you. Their job is to check on you regularly — even at nighttime — to make sure you're comfortable and that everything is working the way it should. They also help coordinate your appointments and make sure your family knows what's going on. If the tube in your arm is ever bugging you, you can tell your nurse and they'll help.
Why did that lady ask me to draw a picture about how I'm feeling?

She's probably the art therapist! The art therapy program at Children's Hospital gives kids a chance to share their thoughts and feelings through creative stuff like drawing, painting, or crafting. You don't have to be good at art — it's not about making something perfect. It's just a fun way to express what's going on inside when it's hard to find the right words. You can draw whatever you want!
There's a clown walking around. Is this a real hospital?

Yes, it's a real hospital! That clown is named Ollie, and Ollie is a therapeutic clown. That's a special person trained to bring play, laughter, and fun to kids in the hospital. Ollie's job is to help make your time here feel a little more normal and a lot more cheerful. Hospitals can feel serious, but having someone like Ollie around reminds everyone that fun and silliness are still allowed!
Someone came in and said they're a resident. Are they living here?

Ha, no — they don't actually live at the hospital! A resident is a doctor who has already finished medical school and is now getting extra training in a special area, like taking care of kids. They work with your main doctor to help figure out the best plan for you. Think of them like a doctor who's still learning even more so they can be the best they can be.
What does the person with the guitar do?

That's the music therapist! They use music to help kids feel better while they're in the hospital. Music therapy can help with things like pain and just feeling more relaxed. The cool part is you don't need to know how to play any instrument or sing well to join in — anyone can take part. You might get to play instruments, sing, or just listen. It's one of the neat things Children's Hospital offers.
A lady said she's a child life specialist. What does that mean?

A Child Life Specialist is someone whose whole job is to help kids and their families handle being in the hospital. They're trained to explain what's going to happen before a procedure so it's not as scary, help you find ways to cope with things that hurt or feel weird, and help you express your feelings through play. They're kind of like your personal guide to making the hospital less overwhelming. If you're nervous about anything, they're a great person to talk to!
Someone new came in this morning and said they're my nurse now. What happened to my other nurse?

Nothing happened to your other nurse — they're totally fine! Nurses work in shifts, so after a certain number of hours, a new nurse takes over. When that happens, the two nurses do something called a bedside shift change report, where they talk about how you're doing and what the plan is. Your parent or guardian can listen in and ask questions too. Your new nurse will introduce themselves, and they'll know all about your care because the other nurse told them everything.
What's a dietitian? Somebody called a dietitian came to talk to my mom.

A dietitian is a person who knows a whole lot about food and what your body needs to stay healthy, especially when you're sick or recovering. They might have been talking to your mom about what kinds of food are best for you right now, or about any special diet you might need. At Children's Hospital, the food you get is actually chosen based on what your doctor and dietitian think will help you the most. If you have favourite foods or things you can't eat, your family can let them know!
A dog came to visit today! Whose dog is that?

That's a therapy dog! Children's Hospital has a special program with St. John Ambulance where trained therapy dogs come to visit kids. The dogs are super friendly and calm, and spending time with them can help you feel happier and more relaxed. They're not regular pets — they've had special training for hospital visits. Pretty cool that dogs can have hospital jobs too, right? If you'd like to know when the next visit is, your care team can find out.
Why is there a person from a pharmacy here? I thought pharmacies are just stores.

Good question! A pharmacist doesn't just work at stores — hospitals have them too. The pharmacist at Children's Hospital helps make sure any medicine you're given is safe and the right amount for you. They also answer questions your parents might have about your medicine, like when to take it or if it might make your tummy feel funny. There's even a pharmacy right here on the first floor of the hospital near the B1 entrance. They're part of your care team, just like your doctor and nurse!
